title: Für Elise
description: Beethoven's Bagatelle in A minor (WoO 59), the most recognised piano piece ever written. Its opening section teaches the hand-off between a left-hand broken chord and a right-hand melody, and it is the piece every learner wants to play first.

arrangements.label: Beginner
arrangements.notes: The famous first phrase only (pickup plus eight bars), written at double note values in 3/4 so nothing is shorter than an eighth; the left hand plays the original A-E-A broken chord as three single eighths and the right hand is single notes with every finger marked.
teachingPoints: Right hand starts with finger 4 on E5 and 3 on D#5; the rocking E-D# figure uses only those two fingers.
In bars 2, 3 and 4 the thumb lands on the melody note (A4, B4, C5), then the hand drops to play the rising C-E-A, E-G#-B and E-E-D# with fingers 1-2-5, 1-3-5 and 1-4-3 (an octave jump for E4 to E5).
Left hand: 5-2-1 on A2-E3-A3 and E2-E3-G#3; practise placing the hand on the bass note during the right hand's trill bar so it is ready on the downbeat.
Count the eighth rest in bars 2-4 and 6-8 out loud; the right hand's rising group must wait for it.

arrangements.label: Intermediate
arrangements.notes: The whole opening A section (pickup through the return of the theme, 23 bars) with the original right hand, while the left hand plays the bass note as an eighth followed by the two upper notes together as a dyad instead of the three-sixteenth broken chord; the left hand's cross-over notes in bars 12-14 are folded into the right hand.
teachingPoints: Bars 8-14 are the new material: A . B-C-D, E . G-F-E, D . F-E-D, C . E-D-C, B . E-E-E; the left hand changes to C major (C3, G3-C4) and G major (G2, G3-B3) under the E and D bars, and bar 12 ends with an E2 and an E3-E4 octave dyad.

Bar 13 is E-E-E6-D#-E-D# with the high E6 on the third sixteenth (finger 5, an octave leap from the thumb); bar 14 alternates D#-E with 3-4 for six sixteenths before the theme returns in bar 15. Practise bars 13-14 slowly as their own exercise.
In bars 9-12 the right hand drops a seventh to the lower note (G4, F4, E4) and comes straight back up with 1-5-4; keep the wrist loose.
Keep the sixteenth rest after each melody eighth silent; the dyad in the left hand lands on the second eighth and must not be rushed.

arrangements.label: Advanced
arrangements.notes: Faithful to Beethoven's text for the full opening A section: the pickup E-D#, the a-b-a form through bar 22, the original left-hand sixteenth broken chords (A2-E3-A3, E2-E3-G#3, C3-G3-C4, G2-G3-B3), the dotted-eighth melody notes of bars 9-11, and the left hand crossing over into the treble (bars 12-14) around the high E6 and the retransition trill.
teachingPoints: The core coordination is the hand-off: left hand plays three sixteenths (A2-E3-A3), then the right hand continues the arpeggio upward (C4-E4-A4) after a sixteenth rest; practise bars 2-4 hands together very slowly until the six sixteenths sound like one line.

Bars 12-14 are the hand-crossing: the left hand rises E2-E3-E4 and then plays the E4 and the lower E5/D#5 (treble clef) in between the right hand's E5, E6 and D#5, so the D#-E alternation of bar 14 is shared between the hands. Learn each hand's notes alone, then let the thumb find B4 on the fourth sixteenth of bar 15 without accenting.
Bars 9-11: hold the dotted-eighth melody note (E5, D5, C5) through the third sixteenth before dropping to G4, F4, E4 with 1-5-4.
Dynamics: pp throughout, with a slight swell in the B phrase (bars 9-12) and a return to pp for the final A.
Finger the melody eighths with the thumb in bars 2-4, 6-8 and 16-21 so the following rising group fits under the hand.
